text_blocks.snippet: While triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) can be cured, particularly in its early stages, it's generally considered more challenging to treat than other breast cancer types. The term "triple-negative" means the cancer cells lack three common receptors: estrogen, progesterone, and HER2, making them unresponsive to targeted therapies that are effective for other breast cancers.
snippet_highlighted_words: can be cured, particularly in its early stages

list.title: Localized or regional TNBC
list.snippet: (contained within the breast or nearby structures/lymph nodes) has a good chance of being cured with treatment.

list.title: Treatment typically involves surgery
list.snippet: (lumpectomy or mastectomy) to remove the tumor, followed by chemotherapy, and sometimes radiation therapy to eliminate remaining cancer cells.

list.title: Immunotherapy
list.snippet: is also increasingly used in combination with chemotherapy, especially before surgery.

list.title: PARP inhibitors
list.snippet: are a newer targeted therapy option, particularly for TNBC with specific genetic mutations (like BRCA1).
TNBC is more likely to recur: after treatment compared to other breast cancers.
For metastatic TNBC: (spread to distant parts of the body), cure is less likely, and treatment focuses on controlling the disease and improving quality of life.
Advances in treatment: (like immunotherapy and targeted therapies) are improving outcomes for TNBC, but more research is needed.
Early detection: through screening is crucial for improving the prognosis of TNBC.
Individualized treatment plans: are essential, taking into account the stage, size, and spread of the cancer, as well as the patient's overall health.
Clinical trials: offer access to cutting-edge therapies and are an important part of TNBC research.

text_blocks.snippet: In summary, while TNBC can be curable in its early stages, it's important to remember that each case is unique, and treatment outcomes can vary.

text_blocks.snippet: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is a type of breast cancer where the cancer cells lack three important proteins: estrogen receptors (ER), progesterone receptors (PR), and human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2). This means that the cancer is not fueled by these specific hormones or proteins, making it more challenging to treat with targeted therapies.
snippet_highlighted_words: a type of breast cancer where the cancer cells lack three important proteins: estrogen receptors (ER), progesterone receptors (PR), and human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)

list.title: Receptor Status:
list.snippet: In normal breast cancer, these receptors are present on cancer cells and can be targeted by therapies. For example, estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer can be treated with anti-estrogen drugs, while HER2-positive breast cancer can be treated with HER2-targeted drugs.

list.title: Triple Negative:
list.snippet: Because TNBC lacks these receptors, it doesn't respond to these common hormone and targeted therapies.

list.title: Aggressive Nature:
list.snippet: TNBC is often described as more aggressive, meaning it can grow and spread more quickly than other types of breast cancer.

list.title: Treatment Options:
list.snippet: While it doesn't respond to hormone or HER2-targeted therapies, TNBC is typically treated with chemotherapy, sometimes in combination with surgery and radiation. Immunotherapy and targeted therapies are also being investigated for TNBC.

list.title: Diagnosis:
list.snippet: TNBC is diagnosed through standard breast cancer tests like mammograms, ultrasounds, and biopsies. The biopsy tissue is then tested for the presence of these receptors.

list.title: Prevalence:
list.snippet: TNBC accounts for about 10-15% of all breast cancers.

list.title: Risk Factors:
list.snippet: While the exact risk factors aren't fully understood, TNBC is more common in women under 40 and Black women.
